title: TDBench: Benchmarking Vision Language Models on Top-Down Image Understanding
claim: Models score unevenly across task categories, and decomposing accuracy into knowing versus guessing shows that raw accuracy overstates real capability.
layout: 2 panels, left radar chart and right grouped bar chart, shared model legend
description: The figure has two plots side by side. The left panel is a radar chart with ten axes, one per top-down task: Attribute Recognition, Object Counting, Scene Understanding, Dynamic Temporal, Object Localization, Spatial Relationship, Object Presence, Attribute Comparison, Hallucination Detection and Visual Grounding. Six models are drawn as translucent coloured polygons: InternVL3-38B, GPT-5, Qwen2.5-VL-32B, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemma3-27B and Claude-4.1-Opus. A legend sits at the lower right of the panel. The polygons peak on Scene Understanding and Object Presence and dip on Dynamic Temporal and Object Counting. The right panel is a grouped bar chart with hatched bars for six InternVL3 sizes, from 1B to 38B. It has four groups: Θ (% questions known), r (P(Correct|Known)), g (P(Correct|Guessed)) and A_adj = Θ·r. The y-axis is Score, from 0 to 1. Bars rise with model size, except g, which stays low. The eye goes first to the colourful radar polygons.
caption: (Left) Accuracy across ten top-down image tasks in TDBench. (Right) Knowledge decomposition analysis from TDBench: % of questions known (θ) measures the proportion of questions a model truly knows; P(Correct|Known) (r) is the model’s accuracy among the questions that it knows; P(Correct|Guessed) (g) is the model’s accuracy among the questions it does not know; and the Adjusted Accuracy (Aadj = θ · r) is the model’s accuracy without lucky guesses.
abstract: Top-down images are critical in applications such as autonomous navigation and aerial surveillance, whereas Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are primarily trained and evaluated on front-view benchmarks, leaving their performance in top-down settings largely unexplored. Top-down image rotations correspond to changes in drone yaw while preserving the scene, providing a natural test of consistency. Yet conventional evaluation protocols based on single-pass accuracy can overestimate model capability due to chance correctness or language priors. Repeated sampling evaluates performance under stochastic decoding on fixed image–question pairs, leaving consistency across these transformations untested. To address these limitations, we introduce TDBench, a benchmark over ten task categories for drone-altitude image understanding, and RotationalEval (RE), an evaluation protocol that evaluates whether answers remain correct across rotated views of the same scene, with directional text adjusted where needed. Human evaluators lose almost nothing going from single-pass accuracy to RE, whereas accuracy drops by 15 to 26 points across representative VLMs. We use an Empirical Mixture Model to compare each model's distribution of correct rotation counts to a difficulty-adjusted binomial-mixture null, splitting the residual into mastery and consistent-failure components. The benchmark is integrated into VLMEvalKit and is publicly available at https://github.com/Columbia-ICSL/TDBench.
